\section{Introduction and related research}
Detailed balance restricts directional dependence while preserving a transparent probability model. This study compares that restriction with an unrestricted chain and an IID baseline, using identical information sets and an unchanged allocation rule. Its contribution is a controlled financial application with explicit separation of probability accuracy, the information used by the allocation, and the cost of implementing that allocation. The reversible estimator itself is established methodology.

Statistical forecast accuracy need not rank decisions by economic value \citep{Granger2000,Diebold1995}. Proper scores evaluate reported probabilities \citep{Gneiting2007}; trading outcomes also depend on return magnitudes, exposure and costs. Predictability and economic value can vary across periods \citep{Pesaran1995}, and small statistical improvements can be economically useful under other portfolio mappings \citep{Campbell2008}. Thus, negative trading results here cannot invalidate probabilistic forecasting generally.

Holding intervals also matter. ETF evidence distinguishes trading from non-trading returns \citep{Kelly2011}. Opening-price pressure is documented among attention-attracting stocks \citep{Berkman2012}; overnight and intraday components can exhibit continuation within periods and reversal across them \citep{Lou2019}. Beta-return relationships differ between night and day \citep{Hendershott2020}, while futures returns can concentrate outside US cash-market hours \citep{Bondarenko2023}. These findings motivate timing discipline, not a universal negative intraday premium.

Time irreversibility has an established econometric tradition: time-domain asymmetry tests \citep{Ramsey1996}, bispectral tests \citep{Hinich1998}, and distribution-based tests without moment restrictions \citep{Chen2000}. Stock-index evidence connects irreversibility with volatility asymmetry \citep{Chen2002}; other representations include multiscale volatility \citep{Zumbach2009} and visibility graphs \citep{Lacasa2016}. Finite-state reversible/irreversible decompositions already exist \citep{McCausland2007}, as do reversible estimation methods \citep{Trendelkamp2015}. Forecast ranking under the present discretization is not a test of market-wide reversibility.

Two questions organize the comparison. First, under identical historical information within each asset, does detailed balance improve out-of-sample state probabilities relative to unrestricted Markov and IID forecasts? Second, do identifiable probability-score gains translate into economic gains under a fixed intraday allocation with two-sided costs? Forecast evaluation and trading evaluation therefore remain separate empirical comparisons. The original experiment is supplemented here by algebraic decompositions, by a reconstruction of the daily panel that allows component, circulation and fixed-half statistics to be computed from recorded paths, and by an independent reimplementation of the constrained estimator. These additions interpret and verify the completed experiment. They are not new prespecified hypotheses, and the reconstruction reproduces the archived estimates rather than replacing them with a different design.

\section{Introduction and related research}
Can a structural restriction improve financial probability forecasts, and does any improvement matter for an investment decision? Detailed balance offers a tractable setting for these questions. In a three-state Markov chain it removes one directional circulation parameter while retaining state dependence. The restriction can reduce estimation variance, but it can also discard predictive information when the data-generating process is irreversible. This study evaluates that trade-off using next-session open-to-close return terciles and a fixed allocation rule for three US equity ETFs.

Statistical forecast accuracy and economic value answer different questions \citep{Granger2000,Diebold1995}. Proper scores evaluate the full probability vector \citep{Gneiting2007}, whereas an allocation uses a particular function of that vector and is also exposed to return magnitudes and implementation costs. Predictability and economic value can vary over time \citep{Pesaran1995}; small statistical improvements can be useful under some portfolio mappings \citep{Campbell2008}. A negative trading result under one mapping therefore does not invalidate probabilistic forecasting generally.

The holding interval makes this distinction especially relevant. Trading and non-trading ETF returns differ \citep{Kelly2011}; opening-price pressure, overnight--intraday return patterns and time-of-day variation in risk premia are documented in related markets \citep{Berkman2012,Lou2019,Hendershott2020,Bondarenko2023}. These studies motivate precise entry and exit timing. They do not imply a universal negative intraday premium or determine the execution cost of the ETFs considered here.

Time irreversibility also has an established econometric literature, including time-domain, frequency-domain and distribution-based tests \citep{Ramsey1996,Hinich1998,Chen2000}. Financial applications connect irreversibility with volatility asymmetry and alternative time-series representations \citep{Chen2002,Zumbach2009,Lacasa2016}. Finite-state reversible/irreversible decompositions and reversible estimation methods are already available \citep{McCausland2007,Trendelkamp2015}. The contribution here is an empirical evaluation of a restriction, not a new estimator or a test of market-wide reversibility.

The design links three comparisons. First, identical historical information within each asset isolates the forecast difference between IID, unrestricted Markov and reversible Markov models. Second, an exact log-loss factorization shows which probability components improve and how the allocation responds to them. Third, a daily-return identity separates fixed half exposure, the probability-driven adjustment and trading cost. Circulation paths, alternative estimation rules and a controlled simulation help interpret the restriction. SPY is the primary application; QQQ and IWM are related-asset extensions rather than independent replications.

The unrestricted chain ranks first on both scores for all three assets, but the statistical evidence depends on the asset and adjustment method. Detailed balance provides no demonstrated log-loss advantage. Under the fixed daily round-trip rule, small incremental gains coexist with large absolute losses at the primary cost. The full-period score ranking also masks deterioration in the later calendar segment. The decompositions, reconstructed-panel checks and simulation are retrospective extensions of the completed experiment; they are exploratory and do not create a new untouched evaluation sample.

\subsection{Inference and its scope}
Paired non-circular moving blocks \citep{Kunsch1989} generate 5,000 resamples with seed 20261113. Block length is 20 sessions in the primary analysis and 10 or 60 in sensitivity checks. Within each comparison, the same sampled days are used for both models. The contrasts are unrestricted minus IID and reversible minus unrestricted; negative score differences favor the first model, whereas positive return and Sharpe differences favor it. Percentile intervals are pointwise unless explicitly labeled simultaneous. An interval containing zero does not establish equivalence.

Three families are distinguished: six log-loss contrasts across the three assets, six Brier contrasts, and an exploratory family of twelve economic contrasts comprising six mean net-return and six Sharpe differences. Each family is adjusted separately using aligned block draws across assets and contrasts (Section~\ref{sec:joint}; Appendix~\ref{app:families}). There is no adjustment across the three families. Component, calendar-segment and alternative-rule intervals remain exploratory and pointwise.

Resampling conditions on the saved forecast paths and does not refit thresholds or model parameters. It measures variation in the realized paired loss or return sequences under the dependence assumptions of block resampling, without regenerating estimation or design selection across new histories. Parameter estimation can affect forecast-evaluation inference \citep{West1996}; no general coverage result is asserted for this expanding-window procedure with changing thresholds. Block-length sensitivity does not resolve structural change, and the related ETFs do not provide independent replications.

\subsection{Controlled simulation of the restriction}\label{sec:simulation}
Section~\ref{sec:circulation} shows that the fitted chains carry circulation but cannot say what the restriction costs. Table~\ref{tab:simulation} answers a narrower, designed question: if the data came from a three-state chain with a stated circulation, how much expected log loss does imposing detailed balance cost at a given training length?

The generating matrices keep a uniform stationary distribution, a diagonal of 0.35 and symmetric off-diagonal flows of 0.325, and add a circulation of 0, $-0.7$ or $-1.4$ percentage points per day by shifting each off-diagonal pair by half that amount in opposite directions. The first value satisfies detailed balance by construction; the third matches the fitted SPY and IWM magnitudes. For each length from 250 to 5,000 states, 500 chains were drawn, both estimators were fitted with the same smoothing, and expected log loss was evaluated against the true matrix. No test period is generated, so the comparison isolates the restriction rather than the rolling pipeline.

Three patterns appear. When the restriction is correct it pays: with zero circulation the restricted estimator is better at every length, by $2.1\times10^{-3}$ nats at 250 observations and $1.0\times10^{-4}$ at 5,000, because one free parameter is removed. The cost of misspecification grows with the circulation and falls with the sample: at $-1.4$ percentage points it is $-6\times10^{-4}$ at 250, $+5.8\times10^{-4}$ at 1,260, $+1.17\times10^{-3}$ at 2,520 and $+1.26\times10^{-3}$ at 5,000, approaching the asymptotic $+1.36\times10^{-3}$. With $-0.7$ the crossover between the two regimes falls between 1,260 and 2,520 observations.

At the training lengths used at the first final forecast (5,522, 3,980 and 3,672 observations) the simulated cost is about $1.2\times10^{-3}$ nats, the same order as the observed reversible-minus-unrestricted differences of 0.7 to $1.6\times10^{-3}$. The simulation is consistent with the observed ranking; it does not establish it. Its scenarios were chosen after the empirical results were seen, the generating process is calibrated to those results, and the experiment omits the dynamic threshold layer. It therefore explains a mechanism under stated assumptions and is not an independent confirmation of the empirical finding.

\subsection{Controlled simulation of the restriction}\label{sec:simulation}
Table~\ref{tab:simulation} examines a designed question: when observations follow a stationary three-state chain with known circulation, how does imposing detailed balance affect expected log loss at different training lengths?

The baseline transition matrix $P_0$ has diagonal entries 0.35, off-diagonal entries 0.325 and stationary distribution $\pi_i=1/3$. Its stationary flow matrix is $S=P_0/3$. The generating flow is $F=S+(j/2)C$, where $C_{12}=C_{23}=C_{31}=1$, the reverse entries are $-1$, and the diagonal is zero. Setting $P=3F$ gives circulation $J_{12}=J_{23}=J_{31}=j$. The scenarios use $j=0,-0.007,-0.014$, equivalent to 0, $-0.7$ and $-1.4$ percentage points of daily flow. For each training length from 250 to 5,000 states, 500 chains are simulated and both estimators are fitted with the same smoothing. Expected log loss is evaluated directly against the generating matrix, with stationary row weights; no finite test path is drawn.

When detailed balance is correct, the restricted estimator has lower expected loss at every listed length. Its advantage decreases from $2.09\times10^{-3}$ nats at 250 states to $1.01\times10^{-4}$ at 5,000. Under misspecification, the relative benefit of variance reduction diminishes with training length and the restriction bias becomes dominant. For $j=-0.014$, the reversible-minus-unrestricted difference rises from $-0.638\times10^{-3}$ at 250 states to $+0.950\times10^{-3}$ at 1,260, $+1.165\times10^{-3}$ at 2,520 and $+1.257\times10^{-3}$ at 5,000. For $j=-0.007$, the sign changes between 1,260 and 2,520 states.

At 5,000 states, the stronger-circulation scenario produces a cost of approximately $1.3\times10^{-3}$ nats, of the same order as the empirical contrasts. This is an order-of-magnitude comparison: the simulation grid does not include the exact initial empirical training lengths of 5,522, 3,980 and 3,672 observations, and the weaker scenario is closer to QQQ's fitted circulation. The scenarios were selected after seeing the empirical results and omit the changing-threshold layer. They illustrate the bias--variance trade-off under stated generating processes; they neither identify the source of the observed ranking nor independently confirm it.

\subsection{Interpretation of the restriction}
The overnight literature supplies context but does not identify IWM's losses: no overnight-return decomposition or causal test was performed. Moreover, positive SPY/QQQ gross results contradict a claim that every intraday allocation necessarily faces negative gross returns. Detailed balance may trade variance reduction against restriction bias. With one restricted parameter and several thousand initial observations, its potential variance benefit may be limited, but this explanation has not been tested. Section~\ref{sec:circulation} reports the unrestricted circulation path, which is negative and persistent throughout the final period, so the restriction is binding at every origin. Neither that persistence nor the simulation of Section~\ref{sec:simulation} identifies lost circulation as the cause of the forecast ranking: the score cost of the restriction lies within its own interval, the path is a single highly autocorrelated sample that cannot separate a population asymmetry from accumulated estimation error, and the simulation is calibrated to the same data it is meant to explain. The 15 synthetic checks in Appendix B assess implementation behavior, not the statistical power of the empirical comparison.

\subsection{Interpretation of the restriction}
The score decomposition identifies which forecasting errors change, the circulation path describes which fitted flow detailed balance removes, and the simulation isolates a bias--variance trade-off under known truth. None of these analyses establishes that population irreversibility causes the empirical score gap. The highly persistent fitted circulation reuses an expanding history, the total log-loss intervals include zero, and the simulation was calibrated retrospectively. Likewise, the overnight-return literature does not explain IWM's intraday losses without an overnight decomposition or a causal design. The computational checks in Appendix B assess implementation and numerical agreement, not empirical power or economic identification.

\section{Limitations and conclusion}
The comparison is conditional on three states, first-order dependence and the estimation rule. Changing terciles omit return magnitudes and alter historical labels across origins. Section~\ref{sec:sensitivity} shows that the direction of every comparison survives fixed cut points, rolling windows and a common start date, but that the unrestricted-minus-IID interval includes zero in five of the fifteen asset-by-rule cases. Section~\ref{sec:stability} shows something sharper: the advantage is concentrated in 2015--2018 and changes sign in 2023--2025, so the full-period average summarises no single regime. Isolating adaptation from discretization would require a design that varies one component at a time. Three related US equity ETFs do not establish broad external validity.

Retrospective vendor adjustments are not a point-in-time feed. Common same-session adjustment factors cancel in $C/O$, but historical revisions and execution uncertainty remain. Cash interest, costs and fills are simplified. The primary cost is a stated scenario, not an empirically estimated ETF execution cost. The nearly constant IID allocation is close to, but is not an exact performance calculation for, fixed half exposure. The component estimates of Section~\ref{sec:components} are computed from the daily records and carry intervals, but they decompose a scoring loss rather than wealth, and no path-level decomposition of returns into forecast-driven and residual parts is reported.

Conditional bootstrap coverage under regime changes is unproven, conventional Sharpe scaling ignores serial dependence, and the familywise adjustment of Section~\ref{sec:joint} covers the six score contrasts only. Brier scores, component contrasts, economic outcomes and the alternative estimation rules remain pointwise, and they are not independent replications of one another. The retrospective internal freeze is not external preregistration. New settings or decision rules would need a separately declared evaluation; analyses of the already examined final sample would be exploratory.

Within these boundaries, the unrestricted chain produces modest probability-score improvements over IID, of which only QQQ's survives familywise correction, while detailed balance offers no demonstrated forecast advantage under any convention examined. The fixed daily round-trip allocation remains unprofitable at the primary cost. Separating fixed exposure, probability adjustment and trading cost explains what the economic comparison measures. The score decomposition locates the forecast gain in the middle-versus-outer component, which the allocation uses only weakly, except for IWM; the circulation analysis shows what the restriction removes; and the simulation indicates that removing it costs about $10^{-3}$ nats at these sample sizes when the circulation is as large as fitted. These are conditional descriptions of one sample; they do not identify a mechanism, and the alternative cut-point and window rules preserve the direction of the comparisons while weakening their precision. The evidence therefore supports a bounded statement about direction, rather than equivalence of the forecast models or a general rejection of probabilistic forecasting for investment decisions.

\section{Limitations and conclusion}
The evidence is conditional on three related US equity ETFs, three return states, first-order dependence and the stated estimation rules. Changing terciles discard return magnitudes and relabel history across origins. Alternative thresholds and windows preserve the direction of the full-period comparisons but reduce precision in several cases. Calendar segments show a more substantive limitation: the unrestricted advantage is concentrated in the earlier period and reverses for SPY and QQQ in 2023--2025. The full-period mean should not be interpreted as a stable forecasting edge.

Data and execution assumptions also limit interpretation. Retrospective vendor adjustments are not a point-in-time feed. A common same-session adjustment factor cancels in $C/O$, but revisions to that ratio can change labels and fitted transitions. The cost scenarios are not estimates of actual ETF execution costs; fills, cash interest and exit notional are simplified. The daily-return decomposition is exact under this accounting but is not an additive decomposition of compounded wealth or Sharpe ratios.

Inference is conditional on saved forecasts, with unproven coverage under structural change and conventional Sharpe scaling that does not correct for serial dependence. Separate adjustments cover the log-loss, Brier and economic families; they do not control multiplicity across all analyses. Component, segment and alternative-rule intervals remain pointwise. The calibration simulation imposes independent draws from a frozen forecast sequence and therefore is not a general test of sequential calibration. The internal design freeze is not external preregistration, and retrospective diagnostics do not supply new out-of-sample evidence. Any selection of a new allocation or estimation rule requires a separately declared evaluation.

Within these limits, the unrestricted model achieves modest average score gains over IID. Log-loss evidence is consistent across the reported familywise procedures for QQQ and sensitive to the procedure for IWM; SPY is not significant after adjustment. Detailed balance has no demonstrated log-loss advantage, and the data do not establish equivalence. For SPY and QQQ, most score improvement concerns middle-versus-outer probabilities, whereas the fixed allocation is locally more responsive to the conditional upper-versus-lower probability. At five basis points per side, daily round trips overwhelm the small incremental mean gains and all nine model allocations lose capital. The practical implication is to evaluate a probability model together with the information used by a decision rule and its implementation costs, while reporting forecast quality, incremental value and absolute profitability separately.

Table~\ref{tab:calibration} reports the observed count-weighted calibration error and a percentile interval from resampling forecast--outcome pairs in moving blocks. It also retains a separate simulation diagnostic: with all saved forecasts held fixed, 500 independent outcome sequences are drawn, each day from its forecast vector. The reported tail fraction is $(1+K)/501$, where $K$ counts simulated errors at least as large as the observed error. Its minimum attainable value is approximately 0.002. All nine values are at most 0.004 under this reference model, without adjustment across the nine diagnostics.

This simulation assumes more than bin-level or sequential calibration. In an adaptive forecasting system, later probabilities depend on earlier outcomes; independently resampling outcomes while freezing the entire probability sequence does not regenerate that dependence. These tail fractions are consequently reported as reference-model diagnostics, not as a generally valid rejection of calibration under serial dependence or regime change. The block-bootstrap intervals and the independent-draw reference distribution also answer different questions; a positive percentile lower bound for this nonnegative error statistic is not itself a calibrated test of zero error.

Realized final-period class frequencies are 29.9/37.3/32.9\% for SPY, 29.1/39.2/31.6\% for QQQ and 32.8/36.7/30.6\% for IWM (rounding can affect the sums). Historical terciles do not force these future frequencies to equal one-third. This imbalance is consistent with a marginal discrepancy for the nearly uniform IID forecast, but comparison with one-third alone cannot attribute the diagnostic for the time-varying Markov forecasts. Marginal calibration compares mean forecast probabilities with realized frequencies; conditional calibration requires more information. Only three to seven class--bin cells contain at least thirty observations, limiting detailed interpretation of the reliability curves.

\section{Computational verification and limitations}
This section distinguishes verification reported in the supplied replication record from checks performed for the present editorial revision. The latter checked manuscript--table consistency, corrected the simulation units and calibration point-estimate calculation, and re-evaluated the calibration summaries on the existing reconstructed forecast files. It did not repeat every model fit, independent-optimizer run or simulation replication described below.
